nameStory: The Scarlet Sea Cucumber gets its name from its brilliant red color that stands out like a ruby against the ocean floor. Unlike the green cucumbers in your garden, this marine animal earned the 'cucumber' part of its name from early naturalists who thought many sea cucumbers looked like warty, elongated vegetables.
description: The Scarlet Sea Cucumber is a striking deep-water marine animal that looks more like a bright red, flattened cushion than the typical tube-shaped sea cucumbers most people know. This fascinating creature has a tough, leathery body covered in small bumps and can grow to about 3-4 inches across. It belongs to a group of animals called echinoderms, making it a cousin to sea stars and sea urchins. You'll find it attached to rocks and hard surfaces on the seafloor, where it filters tiny particles from the water for food.

idTips.label: Bright red coloration
idTips.description: Unmistakable brilliant scarlet to deep red color that looks almost artificial - much brighter than most marine life you'll encounter

idTips.label: Flattened cushion shape
idTips.description: Low, dome-shaped body that's wider than it is tall, feeling firm and leathery to the touch rather than squishy like a typical sea cucumber

idTips.label: Bumpy texture
idTips.description: Surface covered in small, hard tubercles that feel like tiny pebbles under your fingers, giving it a distinctly rough texture

idTips.label: Feeding tentacles
idTips.description: Feathery, branched tentacles that extend from one end to capture food particles - they quickly retract when disturbed

idTips.label: Rock attachment
idTips.description: Always found firmly attached to hard surfaces like rocks or shells, requiring considerable force to remove

habitat: Found in the cold, deep waters off New England's coast, typically at depths of 30-300 feet where recreational divers and fishing nets occasionally encounter them. They prefer rocky bottoms, ledges, and areas with strong currents that bring plenty of plankton and organic particles. You're most likely to see one if you're deep-sea fishing, lobstering, or scuba diving on offshore rocky reefs and underwater cliffs.

seasonality.spring: Active feeding period as plankton blooms increase food availability. Feeding tentacles are frequently extended and visible.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season with tentacles often extended during warmer water periods. Most likely time for divers to observe them feeding.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down as water temperatures drop. Tentacles may be extended less frequently.
seasonality.winter: Reduced activity in coldest water, with feeding tentacles rarely visible. Body remains attached but appears more dormant.

funFact: When threatened, the Scarlet Sea Cucumber can actually expel its internal organs through its mouth as a distraction technique, then completely regenerate them over several months - imagine if you could throw your stomach at a predator and grow a new one!
confusionNotes: The bright red color makes it nearly impossible to confuse with other sea life, but dead or faded specimens might be mistaken for red sponges. Remember: sea cucumbers feel leathery and firm with distinct bumps, while sponges feel soft and porous with tiny holes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'sea cucumber,' these animals are not plants and are completely unrelated to garden cucumbers. The cucumber name comes from the elongated shape of most species in this group, though the Scarlet Sea Cucumber is actually more flattened than cucumber-shaped.
compareHints: Since there are no other Psolus species in New England waters, compare it to other local sea cucumbers which are typically brown, gray, or green and have the classic elongated 'cucumber' shape. The Scarlet Sea Cucumber's flattened form, bright red color, and rock-clinging lifestyle make it unique among New England's sea cucumber species.
